full_judgment:
48. In Fazal Dad vs Crown PLD 1955 152 FC=7 DLR (FC) 176 it has been observed that the evidence of an accomplice has to be considered as a whole, and though the Court starts with the initial presumption against his trustworthiness it may accept his testimony if it is corroborated in material particulars. It is further observed that the rule that insists on corroboration does not require that corroboration must be on all the particulars of the story, nor that there must be corroboration on that part of the story of the accomplice in which he implicates himself and if the independent evidence produced in the corroboration tends to show that the persons named by him were parties to the commission of the offence charged, the Court is entitled to accept his evidence even though there be no corroboration against the accomplice himself. 

 81. One of the cardinal principles of Criminal Jurisprudence which was always to be kept in view in our system of administration of criminal justice for criminal cases is that a person arraigned as accused is presumed to be innocent unless that presumption is rebutted by prosecution on production of the evidence as may show him to be guilty of the offence with which he is charged and Benefit of every Reasonable doubt should be given to the accused. The concept of benefit of reasonable doubt accepted in England as Public Policy has been available to any accused person on the same ground and to the same extent in our country.
